items.name: Press Council of India Norms of Journalistic Conduct (2022 edition)
items.one_line: The Press Council of India code for newspapers, news agencies and journalists: accurate and fair reporting, headlines that match the story, no caste or community tag that plays no part in the story, prompt corrections and right of reply, restraint on suicide, crime and court reporting, and labelled advertorials; also the news code that the IT Rules 2021 name for digital news publishers.

sources.title: Press Council of India: Norms / Guidelines page
sources.supports: lists Norms of Journalists Conduct, 2022 as the current edition, plus norms approved in Council meetings of 17.11.2023 and 28.03.2024; the Council builds the code under the Press Council Act, 1978 for newspapers, news agencies and journalists

sources.title: Press Council of India: Norms of Journalistic Conduct, Edition 2022 (PDF)
sources.supports: Part A norms 1 (Accuracy and Fairness), 2 (Advertisements), 4 (Caste, Religion or Community References), 9 (Corrections), 17 (Headlines), 29 (Paid News), 39(b) (Suicide), 41 (Right of Reply), 43(a) (Trial by Media); Part D complaint procedure (write to the editor first)

sources.title: MeitY: IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 [updated as on 10.02.2026]
sources.supports: Appendix I names the PCI Norms of Journalistic Conduct as part of the Code of Ethics for publishers of news and current affairs content

items.note: Status as read 2026-10-13: the current edition is 2022 (the Council Norms page lists it, plus further norms approved on 17.11.2023 and 28.03.2024 that this pass did not read). It is the Council's self-regulatory code under the Press Council Act, 1978 for print newspapers, news agencies and journalists; the IT Rules 2021 Appendix names the same Norms as the code for digital news publishers (that route is under an interim stay, see comp:it_rules_2021_digital_news_code). Any person may complain to the Council, after first writing to the editor (Part D). Rules a writer must remember: (1) Accuracy: the press shall eschew 'inaccurate, baseless, graceless, misleading or distorted material', report all sides of the core issue, and not set out rumours and surmises as facts; a report based on an FIR that is critical of someone must say it rests only on the FIR and also carry the affected party's version (norm 1). (2) Headlines: 'Headings must reflect and justify the matter printed under them', and a heading that carries an allegation names its source or uses quotation marks (norm 17). (3) Caste and community: an accused or victim 'shall not be described by his caste or community' when it has nothing to do with the offence (norm 4). (4) Corrections are published suo motu, promptly and with due prominence, with an apology for a serious lapse (norm 9); a person affected by a report gets the right of reply, published promptly, with due prominence and free of cost (norm 41). (5) Suicide: no prominent or repeated stories, no method, no site details, no sensational headlines, no photographs, video footage or social media links (norm 39(b)); crime and courts: an accused is presumed innocent and reports should not lead the public to believe in the person's complicity (norm 43(a)). (6) Advertorials similar to news carry the heading 'Advertisement/Advertorials' in bold, and supplements say 'Marketing Initiative' (norms 2 and 29). Victim identity in sexual offences: see comp:india_sexual_offence_victim_identity (not repeated here).

items.name: NBDSA Code of Ethics and Broadcasting Standards and its specific guidelines (News Broadcasters & Digital Association)
items.one_line: Self-regulatory code for member news channels and their digital news platforms in India: accuracy before speed, prompt corrections, facts kept apart from opinion, labelled file footage and reconstructions, no sensationalised crime or suicide, no prejudging of sub judice matters, no derogatory or communal remarks in debates; complaints go to the channel first, then to the NBDSA.

news channel code of ethics India

sources.supports: fundamental principles and principles of self regulation: accuracy and balance before speed, prompt correction of errors in pictures, captions, graphics and scripts, impartiality, privacy, no identification of sexual-assault and child-abuse victims, sting operations as a last resort

sources.supports: no derisive or derogatory statements about individuals, communities or religious beliefs; no communally inflammable statements; allegations not projected as facts without verification; facts kept distinct from opinion

sources.title: NBDA: A Guide to the Complaints Process of the News Broadcasting & Digital Standards Authority
sources.supports: two-tier redressal, 15-day time limits at each step, inquiry target of 3 months, suo motu and emergency powers including removal of content

sources.title: NBDA: News Broadcasting & Digital Standards Regulations (dated 20.06.2024, amended 03.12.2024)
sources.supports: scope (Members and Associate Members only), Code of Conduct = Code of Ethics, Guidelines and Advisories, graded penalties and removal of content from digital platforms

sources.title: NBDA: Guidelines index
sources.supports: list of specific guidelines (court proceedings, sexual assault, children, hate speech, defamatory content, communal colour, social media content, persons with disabilities, LGBTQIA+); only the reportage and anchors guidelines were read in this pass

items.note: Status as read 2026-10-13: self-regulation that binds only Members and Associate Members of the News Broadcasters & Digital Association, for their TV channels and digital news platforms; the Regulations PDF is dated 20.06.2024 with 'Amended: 03.12.2024'. The Code of Conduct is the Code of Ethics plus Guidelines and Advisories. Rules a writer must remember: (1) Accuracy before speed: 'Errors must be corrected promptly and clearly, whether in the use of pictures, a news report, a caption, a graphic or a script' (Code); allegations are reported accurately as made, agency copy is attributed, archive footage is labelled 'file' with the date of first broadcast, reconstructions are clearly marked, and facts are kept apart from opinion, analysis and comment (Reportage guidelines). (2) Crime and courts: do not glamorise or sensationalise crime or suicide, do not show techniques that may tempt imitation, do not prejudge a sub judice matter, no close-ups of dead or mutilated bodies, no identification of victims of sexual crimes against women and children (Reportage 3). (3) Privacy: no disclosure of where a person or family lives without permission; interviews of the injured, victims or grieving only with prior consent (Reportage 5). (4) Harmony: avoid racial and religious stereotyping (Reportage 9); anchors must not make 'derisive or derogatory statements about individuals, communities or religious beliefs' and must not project allegations as facts without verification from a credible source (Anchors guidelines, 2022). (5) Complaints: first to the broadcaster within 15 days of the broadcast, the broadcaster answers within 15 days, then to the NBDSA within 15 days (Guide). Penalties in the Regulations run from warning, admonition or censure to fines of up to Rs 2 lacs for a first violation, rising to 1% of turnover capped at Rs 25 lakhs, with removal or editing of the content on digital platforms and social media.

items.name: IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, Part III and Appendix: Code of Ethics for digital news publishers and online curated content (OTT)
items.one_line: Part III of the IT Rules 2021, administered by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, applies a Code of Ethics to digital news publishers (PCI Norms, Programme Code, nothing unlawful) and to OTT platforms (ratings U, U/A 7+, U/A 13+, U/A 16+, A with content descriptors), with a three-tier grievance system on 15-day clocks; rule 9(1) and 9(3) were stayed by the Bombay High Court in 2021 and the challenges now sit in the Delhi High Court.

sources.title: MeitY: IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 [updated as on 10.02.2026]
sources.supports: rule 2(1)(m) and (t) definitions; rule 8 application; rule 9 Code and three-tier structure; rule 10 grievance time limits; rule 11 Grievance Officer and OTT rating display; rule 12 Level II measures; rules 18-19 monthly reports and 60-day records; Appendix Code of Ethics and content classification; Schedule

sources.supports: Delhi High Court split the batch into Part II and Part III challenges on 14 Oct 2024; next date 13 Jan 2025; other High Courts had granted interim protection to individual petitioners

items.note: Status as read 2026-10-13: Part III is in the MeitY consolidated text (updated as on 10.02.2026) and is administered by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting. On 14 Aug 2021 the Bombay High Court, as interim relief, directed 'stay of operation of sub-rules (1) and (3) of Rule 9' (the duty to adhere to the Code of Ethics and the three-tier structure); on 22 Mar 2024 the Supreme Court transferred the High Court challenges to the Delhi High Court and disposed of the Union's appeals against that interim order by letting it seek relief there. A secondary report (Nov 2024) says the Delhi High Court split the hearing into Part II and Part III and listed it for 13 Jan 2025; this pass found no Delhi High Court ruling on Part III. So never tell a client the Code is enforceable against them through rule 9, and never tell them Part III is struck down: say it is under challenge with an interim stay of rule 9(1) and 9(3). Rules a writer must remember: (1) Who is covered: a 'publisher of news and current affairs content' means an online paper, news portal, news aggregator, news agency or similar, but not newspapers, replica e-papers, or an individual who is not publishing 'in the course of systematic business, professional or commercial activity' (rule 2(1)(t)). (2) News code (Appendix I): the PCI Norms of Journalistic Conduct, the Programme Code under section 5 of the Cable Television Networks (Regulation) Act, 1995, and no content prohibited by law. (3) OTT code (Appendix II): every title is rated U, U/A 7+, U/A 13+, U/A 16+ or A, with the rating and a content descriptor shown 'at the beginning of every programme', and publishers must strive to put the rating on promos; parental locks for U/A 13+ and above, age verification for A. (4) Grievances (rule 10): acknowledge within twenty-four hours, decide within fifteen days, appeal to the self-regulating body within fifteen days, then to the Ministry oversight mechanism within fifteen days; the self-regulating body can require an apology, a warning card or disclaimer, or reclassification (rule 12). (5) A Grievance Officer based in India with contact details shown on the site (rule 11), a monthly compliance report (rule 18), and records of content kept for at least sixty days (rule 19). AI and synthetic content duties of intermediaries are a separate item: comp:it_rules_sgi_2026.

items.one_line: Content and behaviour rules for appearing in Google News, Top stories and other Google news surfaces: Search-wide policies (deceptive practices, manipulated media, medical content and others) plus news rules on ads and sponsored content, misleading previews and transparency (dates, bylines, author and publisher information, contact details).

sources.supports: no markup requirement for Top stories; headline guidance without a number; recommended image size and aspect ratios

items.note: Status as read 2026-10-13 (Publisher Center pages undated; the Search feature policies carry their own dates, from September 2022 to September 2023): to be eligible for Google News or news surfaces, content must follow best practices for article pages and must not break Search overall policies, spam policies or the Search feature policies. Rules a writer must remember: (1) Ads and sponsored content: ads 'shouldn't exceed your content'; sponsored content must not be passed off as independent editorial content, and sponsorship (ownership or affiliate interest, payment, material support) 'should be clearly disclosed to readers'. (2) Misleading content: no preview content that promises details the article does not deliver. (3) Transparency: news sources should provide 'Clear dates and bylines', information about authors, publication and publisher, the company or network behind the content, and contact information. (4) Deceptive practices: no impersonation, no hiding ownership or primary purpose, no concealing country of origin or a government or political interest group affiliation. (5) Manipulated media: no audio, video or image manipulated to represent actions or events 'that verifiably didn't take place'; medical content that contradicts scientific or medical consensus is not allowed. (6) Violations can mean removal from news surfaces or a manual action in Search Console; exceptions exist for artistic, educational, historical, documentary or scientific content. Top stories (decision for this pass): Google says there is 'no markup requirement' and publishers are considered automatically; Article structured data gives no headline length (only 'Consider using a concise title') and recommends images of at least 50K pixels (width times height) in 16x9, 4x3 and 1x1, so Top stories has no text limit and is not a separate platform item. Discover applies the same policy set: see plat:google_discover.
